- If sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and prices are rising, model often fails to recognize reversal; adjust downward early in the forecast horizon.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overshoots; apply a “cool-down” correction to prevent overreaction.
- When sentiment is mixed or neutral (0.33–0.67), model often drifts toward mean reversion; anchor forecast near recent 7–14 day average if no strong sentiment bias.
- If true outcome shows mean reversion after a spike, model tends to continue trend; force a “reversion bias” in forecast if sentiment weakens or sentiment shifts negative.
- For 30-day horizon, model often underestimates volatility in late period; increase forecast variance or add a “tail risk” buffer if sentiment is uncertain or negative.
- If sentiment history shows recent negative sentiment (e.g., -0.33 or 0.00), model often fails to adjust downward; apply a “sentiment lag” correction: reduce forecast by 1–2% per negative sentiment day.
